title: The lost coin (Luke 15:8–10)
hook: a woman lights a lamp, sweeps the whole house for one coin, then throws a party

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lost sheep: a shepherd who left ninety-nine to walk back out after one. Your line was one is worth the walk. Did you reach out to the one who drifted? Day twenty-six.

You know the feeling. Your keys were right here a minute ago. Now they're gone. You check your pockets twice. You lift the couch cushions. You're on your hands and knees with your phone's flashlight, looking under the fridge. And then, there they are. And for about five seconds, you're the happiest person alive. Right after the lost sheep, Luke tells a second story, and it happens indoors. A woman has ten silver coins, and one is gone. So she lights a lamp, grabs a broom, and sweeps the whole house until she finds it. And then she does something nobody does with found keys. She throws a party. Today, the lost coin.
screen: `THE KEYS WERE RIGHT HERE.` → `TEN COINS. ONE GONE.` → `SHE THROWS A PARTY.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the King James: "Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?" The coin is a drachma, a silver coin often reckoned at about a day's pay. Not a fortune, but not nothing. Think of the house. Small, a low doorway, maybe one little window, a floor of packed earth or stone with cracks everywhere. So she lights a lamp in the daytime, and sweeps, and listens for the clink. Why does one coin matter so much? The story doesn't say. Some suggest the coins were her savings, or part of a family set, but that's a guess. The text just says she searches until she finds it. Then the party. "She calleth her friends and her neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." Notice something. A party probably cost more than the coin. That's the point. The joy is bigger than the thing. Jesus ends it: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." And here is the quiet surprise. Yesterday the one searching was a shepherd. Today it's a woman sweeping her kitchen. Christians have long read the shepherd as a picture of God, and teachers since the early centuries have noticed that this story, told right beside it, gives the same searching love a woman's face. Jesus tells it for the same crowd, people grumbling about who he ate with. His answer, twice now: when someone is found, you don't file it away. You call the neighbors.
screen: `TEN SILVER COINS. ONE GONE.` · `A LAMP, A BROOM, UNTIL.` · `A PARTY THAT COSTS MORE THAN THE COIN.` · then, large: `THE SEARCHER HAS A WOMAN'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably and let a breath go. Think back over the past few weeks and look for one small thing you found again. A lost earring. A friend you reconnected with. A habit you picked back up. A good night's sleep after a bad week. It doesn't have to be big. Hold it in mind, and let yourself be glad about it, properly glad, the way she was. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let the gladness sit there for a while. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The lost coin. A woman who sweeps the whole house for one small silver coin, and then calls everyone over to celebrate.
Your line: throw the party. Tell someone today about the small thing you found again, and make a little fuss about it. Day twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 26 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TREASURE AND THE PEARL.`

howItsDone: Christians read the lost coin together with the lost sheep and the prodigal son, the three stories of Luke 15, as pictures of God searching for people and rejoicing when they come home.

original.note: Greek: a drachma, a silver coin. the coin the woman sweeps the house for in Luke 15:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about being careful with money.
what it means: a story about joy. when something lost is found, you call the neighbors.
what a scholar hears: the searcher here is a woman, set right beside the shepherd. Christian teachers since early centuries have read her as a picture of God seeking the lost.

notes: Luke 15:9 KJV begins 'And when she hath found it, she calleth…'; the quotation starts mid-verse at 'she calleth' and the capital S in the source quote is a capitalization choice. Confirm or lowercase.
Drachma 'often reckoned at about a day's pay' — a common estimate. Confirm.
Description of the house (low door, small window, earth or stone floor) is scene-setting, not text. Confirm it reads as retelling.
'Teachers since the early centuries' reading the woman as God (e.g. Gregory the Great's homily reading her as divine Wisdom) is stated without naming anyone; confirm and consider naming.
'A party probably cost more than the coin' is an interpretive aside, not in the text.
